intel_87210a61730c22b9.question: is AI data center growth driving US electricity demand increase?
intel_87210a61730c22b9.current_state: US electric power consumption per capita (World Bank EG.USE.ELEC.KH.PC) ranged 12393.4-13392.7 kWh/capita over 2010-2022 (no AI-specific attribution; series ends before the 2023+ AI data-center buildout). Separately, live-acquired evidence now connects: (1) global data centers consumed ~415 TWh in 2024 (1.5% of world electricity), growing ~12%/yr since 2017, with IEA naming AI as a primary but not sole driver (AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL); (2) IEA forecasts (not observations) of ~945 TWh by 2030 and ~1200 TWh by 2035; (3) a Jevons-paradox dynamic in general cloud computing (Google total energy +3.7x 2016-2022 despite near-optimal PUE), AI_ATTRIBUTION=INDIRECT; (4) ~130 GW stuck in PJM's interconnection queue with ~$3.5B estimated forgone savings, attributed jointly to data centers and electrification (AI_ATTRIBUTION=PARTIAL), framed as a generation/interconnection-queue shortage, not a transmission bottleneck. No source in this corpus gives a numeric AI-only (vs. general cloud/crypto) share of data center electricity demand. [v3 update] Real evidence has since been added for Europe (Ireland CSO: DC share of metered electricity 5%->22%, 2015->2024; EU EED Art.12 500kW+ reporting mandate, policy-only), the US (LBNL/DOE 2024 report: 176 TWh observed 2023 = 4.4% of US electricity, up from 58 TWh 2014, vs. 325-580 TWh by 2028 forecast -- kept as separate OBSERVED vs FORECAST claims), Korea (capital-region grid-connection bottleneck, 91.8% of contracted nationwide DC capacity concentrated in Seoul region per secondary reporting of National Assembly audit material, NOT independently verified against the primary document), and China (IEA ~100 TWh vs Goldman/Bloomberg ~200 TWh for 2024, both kept rather than resolved). Counterevidence acquisition also closed 2 of 3 remaining SEARCH_NOT_RUN directions with real findings (manufacturing/reshoring per Grid Strategies LLC; weather/peak-load per EIA/Ember, flagged as a peak-load-timescale finding distinct from annual TWh/yr demand growth); the DC-growth-without-power-problems region search ran but found no clear evidence either way (an honest negative, not a gap left unexamined). None of this new evidence provides a numeric AI-only share of data-center electricity demand in any geography.

The H1/H3 simultaneous-SUPPORTED outcome is the clearest symptom.

intel/hypothesis/hypothesis_model.py classify_status() is purely evidence-COUNT-based with zero quality/independence weighting (if supporting_evidence and not contradicting_evidence: return SUPPORTED). As of this update it marks H1 (hyp_b0a4bbbc9b601728, 'AI data centers are a significant driver of electricity demand growth') and H3 (hyp_o0_h3_ai_energy_infra, 'recent demand growth results from multiple non-AI factors') BOTH as SUPPORTED simultaneously, even though they represent competing explanations -- because each merely has >=1 supporting claim and 0 directly-contradicting claims in the model's narrow count-based sense. This is a disclosed structural limitation of the current hypothesis model, not a data error and not silently corrected here: classify_status() was intentionally left unmodified this phase per explicit instruction, since rewriting its logic would be an unscoped architecture change. Any report or synthesis reading H1/H3 status must present both as SUPPORTED-under-this-model while explicitly flagging that the model cannot currently adjudicate between competing hypotheses by evidence quality, independence, or directness of contradiction.
